subject: Re: Redwood Dedicated vs Hyperscaler GPU - follow-up & next steps
messages:
From: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.com>
To: Alex Jones <alex.jones@acme.com>, Priya Sharma <priya@acme.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>, Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.com>

Subject: Redwood Dedicated vs Hyperscaler - post-demo recap & proposed next steps

Alex / Priya 	6 thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap from our call and proposed next steps so we keep momentum: 

Key takeaways:
- Primary objective: predictable inference economics + SLA (low tail latency) for public-facing embedding and chat endpoints.
- Main competitor: Hyperscaler-managed GPU endpoints (their reserved instances + autoscaling). Acme cares about both unit cost and guarantees during traffic spikes.
- Constraints: compliance roster requires VPC connectivity and SOC2 evidence; procurement prefers a clear reserved-capacity quote.

What Redwood brings (short):
- Dedicated capacity: reserved GPU pool with guaranteed throughput and isolation (no noisy neighbor variance).
- Flexible burst/buffer: configurable burst bandwidth to handle spikes above baseline without cold-starts.
- Fall-back routing: automated failover to compatible hosted variants if Dedicated capacity is exhausted.
- Observability + per-token cost breakdown for engineering + procurement.

Proposed next tests (to compare apples-to-apples with hyperscaler):
1) Throughput & tail latency sweep (1k -> 5k RPS, 128-token avg) 	6 capture p50/p95/p99 for generation and embeddings.
2) 72-hour soak under production-like traffic shape (prefix caching on, 10	20% cache hit) to measure steady-state cost and KV-cache effectiveness.
3) Cold-start & burst scenarios: ramp from baseline to 3x in <60s to validate burst config.
4) Failure & fallback: simulate capacity outage and confirm routing/fallback behavior and SLA continuity.

Next steps:
- I attached a short deck that maps Dedicated config options to equivalent hyperscaler footprints + a ballpark reserved pricing table.
- If you can share a short list of representative traffic (RPS, avg tokens) and any compliance docs we should be aware of, we	6ll size a POC rig.
- Proposed slot for a hands-on eval: week of Mar 9 	6 we can provision a reserved 8x-A100-equivalent pool for a 7-day POC.

Action items for Acme:
- Share target RPS and token distribution (1	2 paragraphs is fine).
- Confirm whether procurement needs an MPA draft before POC.

Thanks 	6 will coordinate with Lauren + Soojin on setup once we have numbers.

Best,
Markus

Markus 	6 appreciate the clear recap. A few clarifying Qs from our infra team before we lock a POC slot: 

1) Capacity guarantees: when you say "reserved 8x-A100-equivalent pool" 	6 does that come with an SLA for minimum throughput and a promised inability for other tenants to impact our p99s? Any examples of p99 numbers you can share for similar customers?

2) Cost model: hyperscaler reserved instances give us a known committed monthly price; does Redwood Dedicated offer a monthly commit for reserved pools or is it billed daily/hourly with a minimum? We want to do a TCO comparison across a 12-month horizon.

If you can answer the above and confirm a POC start on Mar 9, we can mobilize infra and procurement.

Subject: Re: Redwood Dedicated vs Hyperscaler - answers & POC proposal

Alex 	6 great questions, answered inline below. See also updated notes + POC plan attached.

1) Capacity guarantees: Dedicated is a reserved pool with isolation; you get a contracted throughput baseline (tokens/sec or concurrent requests) and we guarantee noisy neighbors won't affect your p99s because scheduling and NVLink isolation is enforced at the tenant layer. For customers in a similar profile (public SaaS, ~2k RPS), we've seen steady p95 < 120ms and p99 < 250ms for 512-token gen workloads on an 8x-A100-equivalent pool. We can provide anonymized SLA telemetry post-POC.

2) Cost model: we offer both monthly reserved contracts (committed capacity, lower unit price) and short-term reservations for evals. For procurement comparisons, we'll produce a 12-month TCO sheet that maps reserved pool sizes to equivalent hyperscaler reserved instance bundles (we included a ballpark in the attached deck).

3) Failover: fallback to hosted variants is automatic and typically takes 10	30s for traffic rerouting at the DNS/load-balancer level; end-to-end retries are configurable 	6 we can do region-level retries, but cross-region adds latency. We recommend a short grace period with automated retries for user-facing endpoints to mask transient failovers. We'll document exact failover timelines in the SRE runbook for the POC.

4) Test harness: Redwood will provide the test harness (JMeter + k6 scripts + a simple workload generator) and will instrument it to produce the same telemetry we present in our dashboards (per-token cost, cache-hit rates, p50/p95/p99). We'll run the 72-hour soak together and provide a shared Grafana dashboard.

POC ask from Acme (what we need to size):
- Target steady-state RPS (avg) and 95th percentile peak (short bursts).
- Average request token distribution (prompt + generation).
- Any specific models you plan to run (open or private).

Logistics: we can provision the reserved 8x-A100-equivalent pool on Mar 9 for a 7-day POC. If procurement needs an MPA in advance, we'll surface a draft (attached acme-mpa-draft.docx) and can sign an NDA ASAP.

Next: I can run a short internal checklist with Lauren & Soojin tomorrow to ensure infra is ready and we have the harness staged. If Mar 9 works, I'll lock it in and send calendar invites.

Best,
Markus
Senior Sales Engineer | Redwood Inference
